Therefore, when it is said that the reason is "pervaded by one part of the side of the property of the property-bearer to be proved," it comes to be understood that it is pervaded by the property to be proved. If someone asks, "Is not the property-bearer also one part of it?", that is true, but pervasion by it is impossible, because it has the nature of a particular. If someone objects, "Pervasion is merely not understood with respect to the particular; it is not that it is absent," that is not so. For pervasion has the nature of positive and negative concomitance <note>original: "rjes su 'gro ldog", Sanskrit anvaya and vyatireka</note>; these have the nature of being present in every instance; and that is impossible for a particular. Therefore this meaning comes to be understood: the reason is that property of the property-bearer to be proved which is pervaded by the property to be proved. Having explained the words "a property of the subject, a part of it," the word "pervaded" is mentioned in order to explain pervasion. Because the pervaded is pervaded by the pervader, it is called "pervaded." Stating this means stating the distinctive nature of being restricted by those two. Therefore it is stated just according to what kind of distinction the pervader has; the word "to be done" <note>the grammatical form of the term, as if denoting an action</note> does not signify any action at all. Here, in placing a restriction on the three words, three kinds of restriction become possible: "only in that," "only in the qualifier," and "only existing." Of these, since it is reasonable that, in making the pervader understood, the qualified item is what makes it understood, it is taught that "the reason is pervaded by a part of it." It is taught that the pervaded has positive and negative concomitance with the qualifier alone, and that the reason is also what makes known, because it is these very relations that establish it. Therefore, when the nature of what makes known is stated as "the reason makes known, because when the prover is present the presence of what is to be proved is fixed," one should state it as "in that, the pervader is only present." <summary>This page from a Tibetan commentary on Buddhist logic explains why the logical reason must be pervaded by the property to be proved, and why pervasion cannot hold of a mere particular. It then analyzes the three possible restrictions ("only in that," "only in the qualifier," "only existing") implied by the definition of a valid reason.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page, in the middle of a verse passage</meta>nor is it a fourth.
Just as, of a man who has three sons,
because one of his sons is dear to him,
the world says, "He has but one son,"
so too should it be regarded here.

Because of the relation "it does not arise without that,"
it never resides in the three characteristics.
Of the aspect "impossible otherwise,"
one is observed to be present in the reason.

Whatever is "inexplicability otherwise" <note>Sanskrit anyathanupapannatva: the reason cannot be accounted for in any other way than by the presence of what is to be proved</note>,
that alone is the reason.
Whether the two examples exist or not,
they are not its cause.

Where inexplicability otherwise is present,
what is to be done there with the three?
"He is dark-skinned, because he is that father's son,
like the other sons who are seen."

Here, although it has the three characteristics,
it does not serve to establish certainty.
Apart from its two examples,
this is the reason with a single characteristic.

"Entities and non-entities have the nature of existing,
because they are apprehended in some way."
"Because it is called 'the moon,'
the hare-marked one is not a non-moon." <note>The "hare-marked" is a classical Indian epithet for the moon, whose markings were seen as a hare.</note>
This is the second illustration of the characteristic.

Another reason should also be stated:
when what arises from the touch of a mosquito that has landed
comes to be perceived,
one knows with certainty, "This sensation was produced by a mosquito."

In the act of grasping visible form,
the eye is fully endowed with capacity,
because it performs that act,
and because it sees that form.

Further, the self, a pot, and the like
have in some way the nature of non-existence,
because in some way they are not apprehended,
like a horn connected with a donkey.

The horn of a hare and the like, too,
have in some way the nature of existence,
because in some way they are apprehended,
like, for example, the self, a son, and the like.

"Your father too is in this house":
this is to be known,
because the very voice of your father
is heard in this house.

For entities such as sound and a lamp
there is inexplicability otherwise.
Even where there is no property of the subject,
it is seen to be a means of understanding.

Therefore the reason
with a single characteristic is the chief means of understanding.
What use to you is the examination
of other pointless things such as the property of the subject?

That reason which possesses this characteristic,
is it to be understood through a universal,
or is it desired to be known

<summary>This verse passage from a Tibetan translation of an Indian logical work argues that the sole defining mark of a valid reason is "inexplicability otherwise," and that the traditional three characteristics, including property of the subject and the two examples, are neither necessary nor sufficient. It illustrates the point with a series of sample inferences, such as a mosquito's bite known from its sensation and a father known to be home from his voice.</summary>
<keywords>Buddhist logic, pramana, inexplicability otherwise, anyathanupapatti, three characteristics of the reason, trairupya, property of the subject, examples, single-characteristic reason, moon, hare-marked, mosquito, hare's horn, inference, Derge Tengyur</keywords>

The word "སྐྱེས་མོས་" is obscure and is rendered tentatively.</meta>Among these, the one in which nothing undermines its non-deceptiveness is the genuine one. On account of what? "In a dream, again with regard to that same thing or to another." The words "this is" refer to enjoying intense delight. "Because it is known" means: because it is non-deceptive, being experienced as performing its function at that very moment. The meaning, therefore, is that waking and dreaming are valid cognition and its opposite by virtue of being non-deceptive and its opposite.

Someone thinks: "If dream and waking are distinguished as false and true simply by being seen, what need is there for some other cause of the distinction?" In reply the text says "dream and the other." Merely appearing separately does not distinguish the one from the other, because in that respect there is no difference. The meaning is that the distinction between deceptive and non-deceptive would not be established.

Is it not unreasonable to say, <unclear>སྐྱེས་མོས་ཀྱིས</unclear> "because there is no object here, since it does not exist"? For this "since it does not exist" is not an object of apprehension, whereas "it does not exist" is what is apprehended.

Someone thinks: "If it is devoid of any supporting object, no cognition at all would arise." In reply comes the passage "the cognition that this does not exist." "Understood by another" means understood by perception or by inference. Visible form, taste, and the like are understood by the perception in which they appear. Hence their existence does not appear, because it lacks isolation from other things. Since it is simply a nature isolated from that, it is a cognition: even though the faculties suited to such an object do not know it, it knows itself. The bare nature devoid of that, a cognition following upon perception, is conceived as what produces its own aspect. Therefore the words "having become such" show that its object is nothing other than conceptual imagination. <summary>This page from a Tibetan commentary on Buddhist epistemology argues that waking and dream cognitions are distinguished as valid or invalid only by being non-deceptive or deceptive, not by their mere appearance. It then explains how a cognition of absence arises without an external object, its object being conceptual construction.</summary>

"That is not the kind that knows reality." By whom? "By all who do not see the highest": by all those other than the Buddha, whose condition is corrupted by the apprehended and the apprehender. The Buddha alone knows reality; others do not. Although the Buddha, the Blessed One, has fully discerned the very aspect of the inverted, he establishes things just as they are seen. In this way he has taught the cause of those who cling.

If one asks why those who do not see the highest do not know reality, the text says "the apprehended and," and so on. Those who do not see the highest are never without the corruptions of apprehended and apprehender. Because they are always corrupted by the aspects of apprehended and apprehender, such seeing and such corruption are not supreme or exalted. Since they also lack the supreme seeing that is free of the two, by what means could they come to know that reality? It is because the latent impressions <note>Sanskrit vasana: traces left in the mind by past experience</note> of the two have not been uprooted. When they come to see what is free of the two, then they will see reality, because reality has the defining character of being free of the two.

"Therefore," that is, for that reason, "those indifferent to the meaning of reality": the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who have set aside with indifference the meaning of reality, which is free of defining characteristics, "make the elephant's gaze." <note>An elephant was proverbially said to see everything while appearing to look at nothing, keeping its eyes half closed.</note> Like an elephant, although they have already seen the reality of things, they appear as if they themselves do not see it. "Solely by the mind of the world, they engage in the practice of the external." Adapting themselves to the appearance of those who cling to the objects as they appear to the world, they say, "Understand things just as they appear; do not grasp at anything contrary to how they appear." <summary>This page from a Tibetan commentary on Dharmakirti's epistemology explains that only the Buddha, free of the duality of apprehended and apprehender, knows reality. Out of indifference to ultimate reality, the Buddhas adopt an "elephant's gaze" and teach about external things according to worldly understanding.</summary>

<meta>The OCR contains scattered "#" marks inside words, apparently scanning or input artifacts; they are ignored.</meta>Someone objects: "Exclusion should not be accepted as the meaning of a word, because it is refuted." For that reason the text says, "That is deceptive." "That" refers to the word and so forth that is not exclusion. "Is deceptive" means: it is deceptive because it does not act non-deceptively, or it is deceptive because there is no non-deception in it. Why? "Because its relation to real things is broken": there is no relation to any real thing of that sort, and because earlier the real thing defined as a universal and the like, as the meaning of a word, has already been refuted.

Then someone asks: "If that is so, how does a cognition arise from a word and the like that is not the exclusion of others, when exclusion as the meaning of words has been refuted?" The text says, "All cognitions arising from words." Some cognitions arising from words arise as clinging to unreal objects, solely through the force of latent impressions <note>Sanskrit vasana: traces left in the mind by past experience</note> of habituation to conceptual thought that does not accord with how things are. Therefore things do not come to exist or not exist by their power.

Regarding what was said in the passage beginning "of words such as 'object of knowledge,'" the text mentions "words such as 'object of knowledge.'" To whom does one say, "Words such as 'object of knowledge' have nothing to be excluded"? First, if one states a word such as "object of knowledge" on its own, not placed in a sentence and lacking any connection with other words, then it proves what is already established, because it is pointless, since a word on its own is not used. This is shown in the passage "by the thoughtful, abruptly." "On its own" means connected with other words. "Abruptly" means outside of context. For the thoughtful employ words in order to help the listener, and not out of attachment. By using a word on its own, the listener alone would not be helped in the manner whose defining character is the removal of doubt and misapprehension. For if a teacher speaks in order to remove the doubt and misapprehension that have arisen in that listener alone, and to produce a cognition free of doubt, then in that case he will have helped him. Otherwise

<summary>This page from a Tibetan commentary on the Buddhist theory of exclusion (apoha) argues that word meanings not understood as exclusion of others are deceptive, since they lack a relation to real things. It then answers the objection that universal words such as "object of knowledge" exclude nothing, noting that the wise use words in context to remove a listener's doubt.</summary>
<keywords>Buddhist philosophy of language, apoha, exclusion of others, word meaning, universals, deception, conceptual thought, latent impressions, vasana, object of knowledge, doubt, misapprehension, teacher and listener, Derge Tengyur</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>Why must it be said that it is not alone? The proponent of the established doctrine says, "because it is not momentary." That is: whatever moment of its own nature accompanies its co-operating factors and occurs together with them, that very moment, from beginningless cyclic existence onward, is the first moment of its own nature. Therefore its own nature is fixed as momentary. How could it come to be alone?

Here someone may think: "It must also be proved that a thing whose nature is to occur in a single moment produces an effect." For that reason the text says, "How it produces has already been explained." How something that abides for a single moment produces an effect was already explained above, in the passage ending, "they too are neither earlier nor later, nor of a different nature." When this is so, how could a thing endowed with capacity, which produces its effect without interruption and whose nature is to occur in a single moment, become earlier, later, or separate? Since it has the disposition of arising from one single moment alone, it is "something whose nature is to occur in a single moment." Some manuscripts read "something whose nature is to occur in that moment." This means that the words should be construed thus: since it has the disposition of occurring only in that very moment intended here, it is "something whose nature is to occur in that moment." Here "earlier," "later," and "separate" are explained as words for becoming otherwise.

Here someone may think: "Seeds and the like that have not come together are seen to exist earlier, and, when taken out of the assemblage, to exist separately and later. That alone is what is seen to become otherwise." For that reason the text says, "Whatever becomes," and so on. Whatever has not come together, and whatever is taken out of the assemblage and set apart, is not that very thing whose nature is to produce without hindrance. Therefore, as for the consequence that was stated, "Why does a momentary thing not produce alone, why is it not alone?",

<summary>This page from a Tibetan commentary on Buddhist epistemology defends the doctrine of momentariness: a thing that produces its effect exists only for a single moment and so cannot be earlier, later, or separate from its co-operating causes. It also records a variant manuscript reading of a key phrase.</summary>
<keywords>Buddhist philosophy, momentariness, causation, co-operating conditions, efficacy, assemblage of causes, seed, manuscript variants, beginningless cyclic existence, Derge Tengyur</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>it is said that the mind is the example. "Therefore" sums up the refutation of the support.

What need is there to say more? First of all, is the thing that perishes dependent on something else, or not dependent? On the first alternative, a cause that makes that thing remain is pointless, because what does not remain to destroy it itself remains. On the second as well, it is without capacity. The word "they" is a plural form, because the individual instances are meant. If a support makes the perishable remain, whether by itself or through another, then everything that has birth would be endowed with a remaining support. The rest is easy to understand.

Further, is the thing to be made to remain itself perishing or not perishing? Here too, respectively, it is incapable of it and there is no need for it. The difference is that earlier the two faults were set out after examining only the alternative of perishing that the opponent had accepted. "Summary" is meant to be stated with the remainder included. The meaning is that these are verses summarizing what was stated and what is implied by the sense.

In the ultimate sense, abiding in an object is not even contact with the object. Why? The text says, "By the mind." "Its" means of the object. The thought is that the mental consciousness that links to a new birth is itself the sentient being. If someone objects, "Even for a non-conceptual cognition there is nothing beyond the mere aspect of contact with the object," that is true. For a non-conceptual cognition, establishing it as contact is fitting, because there is an experience of the aspect that is clear with respect to that object. For a conceptual cognition it is not so, because it engages by way of both object and aspect. For that very reason the text says "in the ultimate sense."

That in which there is the disposition to become something characterized by the waning and waxing of the lamp: since those are its nature, light and lamp, the material cause and what arises from the material cause, stand as support and supported. How, when that changes, this change is the faultless characteristic of a material cause, has already been shown earlier. Again, repeating

<summary>This page from a Tibetan commentary on Dharmakirti's epistemology refutes the view that the body is a support that makes consciousness remain, arguing that a perishing thing needs no such cause. It then discusses why the mind's contact with an object holds only for non-conceptual cognition, and the lamp and its light as an example of material cause and effect.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>It has already been shown that its existence is that very nature. Someone asks: "Then how can a fire that does not produce smoke be fire, or smoke produced by smoke be smoke?" This fault does not arise, because what we accept is that particular kind of fire and smoke, not fire as such. What is denied is that something other than fire is the cause; it is not held that every fire is a cause. Alternatively, that is not so: it has been shown elsewhere that, because fire is never separated from its capacity to produce smoke, from its very arising onward it never departs from being what benefits that which is to be benefited.

Someone objects: "Since there is also fire that does not produce smoke, is it not the case that fire as such does not produce smoke? Therefore this would become just a particular kind of distinction, like momentariness and the like. So either a distinction would arise even apart from fire-ness, or else you must explain in some other way how smoke does not deviate from fire as its cause."

We reply: although fire-ness is accompanied by distinctions, there is certainly also a distinction that has become its own nature. Otherwise, since fire-ness would be undifferentiated while the distinctions were differentiated, you would have ended up accepting a universal. Therefore, just as things are differentiated by fire-ness, so too they are differentiated as smoke-producing and non-smoke-producing, and so there is no fault at all.

When the "head of Indra" <note>Sanskrit sakramurdhan, a term for an anthill, from which a smoke-like vapour was said to rise; a stock example in Indian logic of something resembling smoke without fire</note> is of a nature that is not fire, then if smoke arises from the head of Indra, which is not a cause of smoke, that would become its cause in the form of fire.

Someone says: "Since things do not arise from what is dissimilar, since difference in causes produces difference in effects, and since what produces smoke is just a form of fire, smoke does not arise from what is not fire. On that ground it is said not to deviate from fire." Then how does smoke arise from dissimilar and different co-operating factors, and from what is not fire? This is what is meant by the words "Then now, from different co-operating factors." Those, being different, are dissimilar and have a nature that is not fire. <summary>This page from a Tibetan commentary on Buddhist logic defends the inference of fire from smoke: what the inference relies on is a particular kind of fire with the capacity to produce smoke, not fire as a bare universal. It then answers the objection that smoke-like vapour from an anthill, or smoke from dissimilar co-operating causes, breaks the invariable relation.</summary>

Scattered "#" marks are input artifacts and are ignored.</meta>its nature cannot be determined to be its object. Because that conceptual thought arises from latent impressions <note>Sanskrit vasana: traces left in the mind by past experience</note> produced by cognitions of existence, of non-existence, and of both, it is described, by virtue of clinging to the aspect that appears in it, as a property of a real thing, of a non-thing, or of both. Therefore people consider, in terms of existence and non-existence, whether this object that appears from the word <term>pradhana</term> <gloss>primordial matter, the first principle of the Samkhya school</gloss>, as used by those who hold to that subject, has a real thing as its material cause or not. In proving that it does not have a real thing as its material cause, that object, which cannot be dismissed because it is known by each person's own awareness, is the subject.

One cannot say that this object is a particular <note>Sanskrit svalaksana: a unique, causally efficient real thing</note>, because that would not be excluded even for objects not yet attained and objects that have ceased, and because the appearance of clinging to an inverted form of real things also occurs in the cognitions of other, non-Buddhist <term>tirthikas</term> <gloss>followers of rival Indian schools</gloss>.

If words engaged solely with the ultimately real,
then for the objects of other kinds of views
words would not engage without a cause;
and since, concerning the past and the unborn as well,
no statement whatever
would have a false object,
these are held to have objects of the mind as their domain.

These are summarizing verses. Here, in proving that something does not have a material cause of the nature one supposes, the proving property is not unestablished, since there is such a property of non-apprehension. Nor is the object that appears in verbal conceptual thought being denied here, because words are applied to an object placed in the mind, and without it that would be impossible.

Further:

Those who do not dispute the meaning of words
should examine the real thing itself
by the distinction of the alternatives of existence and non-existence,
since the arising of effects depends on it.

Whether the meaning of a word exists or not, no human aim is in the least lost or achieved by it, because it is not reality in the way it is clung to, and because reality

<summary>This page from a Tibetan commentary on Dharmakirti's epistemology argues that the object of a word, such as the Samkhya "primordial matter," is a mental construct rather than a real particular, and so can serve as the subject of an inference about existence. Summary verses conclude that words concern objects of the mind, while real things must be examined for their causal efficacy.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>and so on, there would be no cognition of the variegated. In a painting and the like there is no single nature of a whole <note>Sanskrit avayavin: the whole as a substance distinct from its parts, posited by the Nyaya-Vaisesika school</note>. If one asks, "Then what is there?", the opponent answers: "There is a variegated conjunction <note>Sanskrit samyoga: contact or conjunction, counted as a quality in Vaisesika</note> of blue and the other colours, and what it produces is the cognition of that." That is not the right understanding.

For the conjunction is not variegated. Why? "Because it has no colour." A conjunction, being a quality, does not possess a further quality called colour, because qualities do not have qualities.

Someone objects: "Even though the object of the word is in no way the nature of a variegated conjunction, it shares a property with the variegated nature of the whole found in a variegated butterfly and the like. Therefore, like the variegated, it is called variegated by figurative transfer." The reply is: "A mere figurative designation is no support." The word "conjunction" is to be supplied here: a conjunction is not an object of figurative designation. If it is called variegated because it resembles the variegated, then consider: in a butterfly there is no variegated nature of a whole, and in each of the individual parts there is not the slightest ground for figuratively designating variegation. If one says, "Both together are the ground for designating a difference in nature," that is not so, because there is no variegation in the variegated form of the butterfly, and because in a painting and the like there is also no variegated nature.

Further, if it were held to be a figurative designation because in a painting and the like the conjunction inheres in a single object <note>Sanskrit ekarthasamavaya: co-inherence in one substrate</note>, that too is not reasonable. In that case, where there is inherence and conjunction in the parts such as blue, there is no variegated conjunction in each of those parts individually; rather, what exists there is their own nature as blue and so on, "because each one is variegated." And because there is no relation to a single object, a merely designated object is not reasonable either.

Someone says: "That may well be so. But in a painting and the like, the seeing of the parts such as blue arises in succession, and then a variegated cognition arises that blends them, thinking, 'This is a single variegated nature.'"

<summary>This page from a Tibetan commentary on Buddhist epistemology refutes the Nyaya-Vaisesika claim that the cognition of a multicoloured object, such as a painting or a butterfly, is caused by a variegated whole or a variegated conjunction. It argues that a conjunction, being a quality, cannot have colour, and that calling it variegated by figurative transfer has no basis.</summary>
<keywords>Buddhist epistemology, Nyaya-Vaisesika, variegated cognition, whole and parts, avayavin, conjunction, samyoga, quality, guna, figurative designation, inherence, samavaya, painting, butterfly, colour, Derge Tengyur</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>is taught as purified; the meaning is that it is stated clearly. The explanation is the passage beginning "What particular transformation…". "From what cause" means from that which makes known; the object of observation is connected. Even when one relies on the word "whose," "from that cause" is supplied from within the sense, and it should be joined thus: "when that very thing is observed to be the cause of hatred and the rest as well." Alternatively, "from what cause" connects with what precedes: it is to be construed as "what particular transformation," namely, depending on which cause of desire and the rest, such as wind and the others. "At that time" means: at that time, relying on the word "whose," one places "that cause" first and construes it as "the nature of all." Since desire and the rest are not invariably bound to bile and the rest, they are not the nature of all; and the particular state residing in bile and the rest would also become the nature of all the particulars, desire and the rest, because the deviation is the same. "For which reason" means: by that cause through which desire and the rest are manifest as equal. If one thinks, "How is it unreasonable?", that too

is stated: it is the particular state of transformation of phlegm and the rest. Even if some particular of wind and the others, whichever it may be, is the cause, not every particular would be accompanied by all of desire and the rest; for since a definite effect is seen at all times, it is to be inferred. The anticipation of the objection, "Because it has a definite particular as its cooperating condition," is the passage beginning "But the effect…". In that case, the particular that is the definite cooperating cause is habituation alone, since the divisions of desire and the rest are seen to follow from its divisions. The reply, "If another cause were imagined, smoke too would not be established as having fire as its cause," is the passage beginning "What smoke, where fire is not seen…". If one thinks, "Because smoke is accompanied by fire, fire is present in that place; therefore fire itself is the cause of smoke, but the locus is not," then the objection "No…"

<summary>This page of a commentary on Buddhist epistemology explains a root-text passage arguing that desire, hatred and other passions cannot simply be produced by the bodily humors (wind, bile, phlegm), since their occurrence does not track the humors. The commentator concludes that the decisive cooperating cause is habituation, and defends the point with the classic example of smoke and fire.</summary>
<keywords>Derge Tengyur, pramana, Buddhist epistemology, commentary, desire, hatred, passions, humors, wind, bile, phlegm, habituation, cause and effect, smoke and fire, inference</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page; the verse quoted begins mid-word ("…whose nature is cessation")</meta>"…whose nature is the cutting off," and so on. Destruction is of two kinds: that whose nature is the cutting off of the continuum, and that whose defining mark is the arising of a dissimilar continuum. Now, if one speaks with reference to destruction whose nature is the cutting off of the continuum, that is not reasonable, for regarding the statement "it does not exist even at the end," why does one say, "Since it has no nature, how could it come to be even at the end?" Therefore, since this is not accepted as existing even occasionally, the consequence that there would be no entity at the beginning and at the end is simply irrelevant. Likewise, when birth occurs through the linking of another moment of similar kind, this is purely a negation. When a pot or the like is about to be destroyed, the meaning is "that very thing does not arise"; it does not establish anything at all about it. How many years after full ordination may one act as a teacher of dependence? "One who has not completed ten years since full ordination should not remain without a preceptor or teacher of dependence." Then may everyone who has completed ten years do these three things? "Not if he possesses none of the pentads set out below." That is, even after completing ten years, if he possesses none of the groups of five set out below, he may not do the three things mentioned above.

What are those groups of five? "Being able to do, or to have done, the following: nursing the sick, removing doubts, turning back one who has fallen into wrong views, and sending away discontent." That is, whether he can do these four named things himself, or can entrust them to another, it is permitted. Here, "nursing the sick" shows that he is patient in suffering and endowed with compassion. "Removing doubts" shows that he is skilled in the Vinaya. "Turning back one who has gone astray into views" shows that he is skilled in the Abhidharma. "Sending away discontent" shows that he understands the thoughts of others.

The phrase "being able to have it done" does not indicate that he cannot do it himself. Why is that?
